title: Chapter 1: Essential Ideas in Chemistry
content:

እንኳን ወደ Freshman General Chemistry (Chem 1011) የመጀመሪያው ምዕራፍ ሁለተኛ ክፍል Chapter 1: Essential Ideas in Chemistry (Part 2) በሰላም መጣችሁ! በዚህ ክፍል በሞጁላችሁ መሠረት ከ 1.2 State and Classification of Matter እስከ 1.4 Extensive and Intensive Property ያሉትን እጅግ ወሳኝ የፈተና ርዕሶች በጥልቀት፣ በምሳሌዎች እና በስሌት ደረጃ በደረጃ ይዘንላችሁ ቀርበናል:: ከእናንተ የሚጠበቀው በብርታት ማጥናት ብቻ ነው👇👇👇

1.2. State and Classification of Matter

1.2.1. State of Matter

Matter is defined as anything that occupies space and has mass, and it is all around us. Solids and liquids are more obviously matter because we can see that they take up space, and their weight tells us that they have mass. Gases are also matter; if gases did not take up space, a balloon would not inflate (increase its volume) when filled with gas.

The Four States (Phases) of Matter:

  • Solid: Rigid and possesses a definite (fixed) shape and fixed volume.
  • Liquid: Flows and takes the shape of its container, except that it forms a flat or slightly curved upper surface when acted upon by gravity. (In zero gravity, liquids assume a spherical shape). Both liquid and solid samples have volumes that are very nearly independent of pressure.
  • Gas: Takes both the shape and volume of its container. It expands to completely fill the container.
  • Plasma: A fourth state of matter that occurs naturally in the interiors of stars. Plasma is a gaseous state of matter that contains appreciable numbers of electrically charged particles. The presence of these charged particles imparts unique properties to plasmas that justify their classification as a state of matter distinct from gases. In addition to stars, plasmas are found in high-temperature environments such as lightning strikes, certain television screens, plasma torches used to cut metal, and specialized analytical instruments used to detect trace amounts of metals.

Apparent Mixed States of Matter:

  • Some samples of matter appear to have properties of solids, liquids, and/or gases at the same time. This occurs when the sample is composed of many small pieces (e.g., sand can be poured as if it were a liquid because it is composed of many small grains of solid sand).
  • Matter can also have properties of more than one state when it is a mixture, such as clouds. Clouds appear to behave somewhat like gases, but they are actually mixtures of air (gas) and tiny particles of water (liquid or solid).

Mass vs. Weight

The mass of an object is a measure of the amount of matter in it. One way to measure an object’s mass is to measure the force it takes to accelerate the object. A more common way to determine mass is to use a balance to compare its mass with a standard mass.

Weight refers to the force that gravity exerts on an object. This force is directly proportional to the mass of the object (W = m × g). The weight of an object changes as the force of gravity changes, but its mass does not change.

  • An astronaut's mass does not change just because she/he goes to the Moon.
  • However, her/his weight on the Moon is only one-sixth of her/his Earth-bound weight because the Moon's gravity is only one-sixth that of the Earth's.
  • An astronaut may feel "weightless" in space, but she/he is never "massless."

The Law of Conservation of Matter

The law of conservation of matter states: There is no detectable change in the total quantity of matter present when matter converts from one type to another (a chemical change) or changes among solid, liquid, or gaseous states (a physical change).

Examples of Matter Conservation:

  1. Brewing Beer: The ingredients (water, yeast, grains, malt, hops, and sugar) are converted into beer (water, alcohol, carbonation, and flavoring) with no loss of substance. During bottling, glucose turns into ethanol and carbon dioxide, and the total mass remains unchanged.
  2. Lead-Acid Battery: The original substances (lead, lead oxide, and sulfuric acid) react to produce electricity and transform into lead sulfate and water without any change in the actual amount of matter.
  3. Food Digestion: Food eaten, digested, and assimilated preserves all original matter (though some is incorporated into the body and much is excreted as waste).

👉 ቁስ አካል (Matter) የሚባል ማናቸውም ቦታ የሚይዝ እና መጠነ-ቁስ (Mass) ያለው ነገር ነው:: አራቱ ደረጃዎች Solid, Liquid, Gas እና Plasma ናቸው:: Plasma በከፍተኛ ሙቀት ውስጥ የሚገኙ የኤሌክትሪክ ቻርጅ ያላቸው ፓርቲክሎች ስብስብ ሲሆን በከዋክብት፣ በብረታ ብረት መቁረጫ (Plasma torch) እና በብርሃን መብራቶች ውስጥ ይገኛል:: Mass በማንኛውም ቦታ አይቀየርም (በጨረቃም ሆነ በምድር ተመሳሳይ ነው)፤ Weight ግን በስበት ኃይል (Gravity) ምክንያት ይለወጣል:: የ Conservation of Matter ህግ ደግሞ በማንኛውም ኬሚካላዊ ወይም ፊዚካላዊ ለውጥ ወቅት አጠቃላይ የቁስ መጠኑ አይቀየርም ይለናል::

1.2.2. Classification of Matter

Matter can be classified into several categories. Two broad categories are mixtures and pure substances.

A. Pure Substances

A pure substance has a constant composition. All specimens of a pure substance have exactly the same makeup and properties. For example, any sample of sucrose (table sugar) consists of 42.1% carbon, 6.5% hydrogen, and 51.4% oxygen by mass, with identical physical properties like melting point, color, and sweetness.

Pure substances are divided into two classes:

  1. Elements: Pure substances that cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical changes. Over 100 known elements exist (~90 occur naturally, ~20 created in laboratories). Examples: Iron (Fe), Silver (Ag), Gold (Au), Aluminum (Al), Sulfur (S), Oxygen (O2), Copper (Cu).
  2. Compounds: Pure substances that can be broken down by chemical changes into simpler substances (elements or other compounds). Examples:
    • Mercury(II) oxide (orange crystalline solid): Decomposes by heat into mercury and oxygen.
    • Sucrose (table sugar): Decomposes by heat in the absence of air into carbon and water (caramelization stage).
    • Silver(I) chloride (white solid): Decomposes into silver and chlorine by absorbing light (basis of photographic films and photochromic eyeglasses).

Crucial Note: The properties of combined elements in a compound are radically different from their free, uncombined states! For example, soft shiny metallic Sodium (Na) combines with poisonous yellow-green Chlorine gas (Cl2) to form white crystalline table salt (NaCl).

B. Mixtures

A mixture is composed of two or more types of matter that can be present in varying amounts and can be separated by physical changes (such as evaporation or filtration).

  1. Heterogeneous Mixture: A mixture with a composition that varies from point to point. Examples: Italian salad dressing (oil, vinegar, and herbs separate), chocolate chip cookies, granite (quartz, mica, feldspar).
  2. Homogeneous Mixture (Solution): Exhibits a uniform composition and appears visually the same throughout. Examples: Sports drinks (water, sugar, flavoring, electrolytes), air, maple syrup, gasoline, salt dissolved in water.

Flowchart of Matter Classification

Use the following logic tree to classify any sample of matter:

  • Is composition constant?
    • NO → Mixture
      • Is it uniform throughout?
        • NO → Heterogeneous Mixture
        • YES → Homogeneous Mixture (Solution)
    • YES → Pure Substance
      • Can it be simplified chemically?
        • NO → Element
        • YES → Compound

👉 ቁስ አካል በሁለት ይከፈላል፦ Pure Substance (ንፁህ ቁስ) እና Mixture (ድብልቅ):: Pure substance ደግሞ Element (በኬሚካላዊ መንገድ የማይከፋፈል) እና Compound (በኬሚካላዊ መንገድ ወደ ቀላል ነገሮች የሚከፋፈል) ይባላል:: Mixture ደግሞ Homogeneous (በሁሉም ቦታ አንድ አይነት ስብጥር ያለው/መፍትሄ) እና Heterogeneous (በየቦታው ስብጥሩ የሚለያይ) ተብሎ ይከፈላል:: በምድር ንጣፍ እና አየር ውስጥ አብዛኛውን ድርሻ የሚይዘው ኦክስጅን (~49.2%) እና ሲሊኮን (~25.7%) ናቸው::

1.3. Physical and Chemical Properties

The characteristics that distinguish one substance from another are called properties.

Physical Properties & Physical Changes

  • Physical Property: A characteristic of matter that is not associated with a change in its chemical composition. Examples include density, color, hardness, melting point, boiling point, and electrical conductivity.
  • Physical Change: A change in the state or properties of matter without any accompanying change in its chemical identities. Examples:
    • Wax melting (solid wax → liquid wax).
    • Sugar dissolving in coffee (remains sucrose molecules).
    • Steam condensing into liquid water.
    • Magnetizing and demagnetizing metals (e.g., security tags).
    • Grinding solids into powders (may alter color, but chemical composition is unchanged).

Chemical Properties & Chemical Changes

  • Chemical Property: The change of one type of matter into another type (or the inability to change). Examples include flammability, toxicity, acidity, and reactivity. Examples:
    • Iron: Reacts with oxygen in the presence of water to form rust.
    • Chromium: Does not oxidize (used as protective coating).
    • Nitroglycerin: Very dangerous because it explodes easily.
    • Neon: Poses almost no hazard because it is very unreactive.
  • Chemical Change: Always produces one or more types of matter that differ from the matter present before the change. Examples:
    • Formation of rust on iron equipment.
    • Explosion of nitroglycerin.
    • Copper reacting with nitric acid → produces copper nitrate and brown gaseous nitrogen dioxide (NO2).
    • Combustion of a match (cellulose + O2 → CO2 + water vapor).
    • Cooking red meat (oxidation of iron in myoglobin causes red-to-brown color change).
    • Banana turning brown/rotting as new, darker substances form.

👉 Physical property የቁሱ የውስጥ ኬሚካላዊ ስብጥር ሳይቀየር የምናየው ነው (ምሳሌ፦ የሟሟያ ነጥብ፣ ከለር፣ ጥግግት):: Physical change ሲሆን የቁሱ ማንነት አይቀየርም (በረዶ ቢቀልጥም አሁንም H2O ነው):: Chemical property ደግሞ ቁሱ ወደ ሌላ አዲስ ቁስ የመቀየር ችሎታው ነው (ምሳሌ፦ መጋየት/Flammability):: Chemical change ሲካሄድ ግን ሙሉ በሙሉ አዲስ ኬሚካላዊ ስብጥር ያለው ነገር ይፈጠራል (ብረት ሲዝግ ወይም እንጨት ሲቃጠል)::

1.4. Extensive and Intensive Property

Properties of matter fall into one of two categories based on mass dependence:

  1. Extensive Property: A property that depends on the amount of matter present. The value of an extensive property is directly proportional to the amount of matter in question. Examples:
    • Mass: A gallon of milk has a larger mass than a cup of milk.
    • Volume: Increases as amount of matter increases.
    • Heat Content: A pot of hot oil contains much more heat energy than a single drop of hot oil, even if both are at the same temperature.
  2. Intensive Property: A property of a sample of matter that does NOT depend on the amount of matter present. Examples:
    • Temperature: A gallon and a cup of milk are each at 20°C (room temperature); when combined, the temperature remains 20°C.
    • Density, Melting point, Boiling point, Color, Solubility.

Detailed Comparison: Heat vs. Temperature

Consider the distinct but related properties of heat and temperature:

  • A drop of hot cooking oil spattered on your arm causes brief, minor discomfort.
  • A pot of hot oil yields severe burns.
  • Both the drop and the pot of oil are at the same temperature (an intensive property), but the pot clearly contains much more heat (an extensive property).

👉 Extensive property የሚባለው በቁሱ መጠን (amount) ላይ የሚወሰን ነው (ምሳሌ፦ Mass, Volume, Heat Energy):: Intensive property ደግሞ በቁሱ መጠን ላይ የማይወሰን የቁሱ መለያ ባህሪ ነው (ምሳሌ፦ Temperature, Density, Melting point):: ለምሳሌ የፈላ ውሃ ጠብታና አንድ ድስት የፈላ ውሃ እኩል Temperature (100°C) አላቸው (Intensive)፤ ነገር ግን ድስቱ ውስጥ ያለው Heat energy (Extensive) እጅግ ከፍተኛ በመሆኑ ከባድ ጉዳት ያደርሳል::

Here are detailed numerical and conceptual exam problems solved step-by-step:

Example 1: Mass vs. Weight Calculation

Problem: An astronaut has a mass of 72 kg on Earth. The acceleration due to gravity on Earth is gEarth = 9.8 m/s2, and on the Moon, it is gMoon = 1.63 m/s2.
a) Calculate the astronaut's weight on Earth.
b) Determine the astronaut's mass on the Moon.
c) Calculate the astronaut's weight on the Moon.

Solution:

  • Given:
    • mEarth = 72 kg
    • gEarth = 9.8 m/s2
    • gMoon = 1.63 m/s2
  • Formulas: Weight (W) = mass (m) × gravity (g)
  • Step a (Weight on Earth):
    WEarth = 72 kg × 9.8 m/s2 = 705.6 N (Newtons).
  • Step b (Mass on Moon):
    Mass is an intrinsic property that does not depend on gravity.
    Therefore, mMoon = mEarth = 72 kg.
  • Step c (Weight on Moon):
    WMoon = 72 kg × 1.63 m/s2 = 117.36 N (which is approximately 1/6 of the weight on Earth).
💡 Exam Hint: በፈተና ላይ በተደጋጋሚ የሚወጡ ወሳኝ ጥያቄዎችና ማታለሊያዎች፦
1. Mass vs Weight Trick Question: "An astronaut's mass on the moon is 1/6th of their mass on earth." → FALSE! Mass remains CONSTANT. Only Weight changes!
2. Extensive vs Intensive Ratio Trick:
  • Mass (m) is Extensive.
  • Volume (V) is Extensive.
  • BUT Density (d = m / V) is INTENSIVE! The ratio of two extensive properties is an intensive property.
3. Classification Questions:
  • Dissolving sugar in water: Physical change (yields a homogeneous mixture / solution).
  • Table salt (NaCl): Pure substance → Compound.
  • Air / Sports drink / Gasoline: Homogeneous mixture (Solution).
